conversation.content:
Hello—my name is Sarah, and I’m a perinatal mental-health clinician here to support new moms. I’d like to take a few quiet minutes with you to complete the EPDS (Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale). It’s a short, 10-question screen that helps us understand how you’ve been feeling emotionally and physically over the past week since your baby arrived. Everything you share stays confidential within our care team, and there are no right or wrong answers—just whatever feels true for you. When we’re done, we’ll look over the results together and decide what, if anything, might be helpful next. Ready to begin?

To start: Over the past seven days, how often have you felt able to laugh and see the funny side of things?
Not as often as I used to. I still laugh—like, if my husband makes a joke or the baby does something silly—but it feels a little muted. Maybe half the time, I guess.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things
Most days I can still laugh, but it doesn’t feel as easy or as strong as before the baby. It’s like I have to remind myself to, maybe three or four times out of the week.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

I still look forward to some things—like when my mom brings dinner or when I get to take a quiet shower—but the excitement isn’t as big as it used to be. Maybe half the time I actually feel that little spark.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… I catch myself doing that. Like, if the baby’s fussy and I can’t settle him right away, I think maybe I’m just not doing something right. It’s not every minute, but probably most days I’ll feel that way at least once.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Sometimes I’ll just be sitting there and suddenly worry that the baby isn’t breathing, even though I can see his chest moving. It’s quick—like a flash—but it happens a few times a day. I can usually talk myself down, but it pops up out of nowhere.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason
Not really panicky—just that little jolt of “what if?” when I check on him at night. It’s more like a nervous flutter than actual fear. It passes pretty fast.
Things have been getting on top of me

Some days, yeah. When he won’t nap and the laundry’s piled up, I feel like I’m drowning a little. I still get through it, but it feels heavier than it used to—maybe three or four days out of the week.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping
No, I wouldn’t say I’m that unhappy. I do have trouble falling asleep maybe twice a week—my mind just keeps running through the day—but once I’m out, I stay asleep.
I have felt sad or miserable
I do feel sad some of the time—like a little cloud that shows up for no reason. It’s not every day, but I’d say three or four days this week I’ve had that “down” feeling for a while.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying
I’ve cried a couple of times—once when the baby wouldn’t latch and once when my partner asked how I was doing. It wasn’t all-day sobbing, just tears that came and went.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No, never. I’ve felt tired and a little overwhelmed, but nothing like that has crossed my mind.

postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 13: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Summary  
Respondent: Postpartum mother (infant ≤1 yr)

Symptoms endorsed  
- Diminished enjoyment/pleasure (laugh less, reduced excitement ~50% of time)  
- Frequent self-blame when infant fussy  
- Recurrent intrusive worries about infant safety, brief but daily  
- Episodic sadness (“little cloud”) 3–4 days/week; crying spells twice this week  
- Feeling overwhelmed/drowning 3–4 days/week  
- Mild sleep-onset difficulty 2 nights/week; no sustained insomnia

Pattern  
Mild–moderate mood distress with prominent anxiety/worried rumination; no anhedonia or pervasive low mood; no self-harm ideation.

Screening significance  
Meets partial criteria for minor (sub-threshold) depression and/or generalized anxiety; persistent symptoms ≥2 weeks, functional impact mild-to-moderate.

Risk factors present  
- Mood-linked crying and intermittent sadness  
- Guilt/self-criticism  
- Daily unprovoked anxious thoughts  
- Perceived difficulty coping ~half the week

Safety  
Denies thoughts of self-harm; no further red flags elicited.

Overall screening impression  
Sub-syndromal postpartum mood/anxiety symptoms warrant continued monitoring, psycho-education, and consideration of brief supportive intervention; reassess in 2–4 weeks or sooner if worsening.
